name: BIO-key International, Inc.

profile.description: BIO-key International sells biometric and passwordless identity and access management (IAM) software, including the PortalGuard IAM platform, MobileAuth (PalmPositive, FacePositive), and Passkey:YOU FIDO2 authentication, plus fingerprint hardware. Its customers are mainly government, defense, and financial institutions [1][2]. Q2 2026 revenue rose 13% to $1.92M (1H 2026 +23% to $4.07M). The company did a 1-for-10 reverse split on April 30, 2026 and regained Nasdaq compliance in July after being flagged for late filings [1][3]. Market cap is about $5.5M [5].

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): BIO-key's main change has been a gradual shift from hardware toward software licensing. Q2 2026 license fees rose 53% to $1.23M while hardware fell 19% to $460K, and gross margin rose to 87% from 73%. Passkey:YOU and MobileAuth palm and face options are incremental product additions rather than a new revenue stream [1][2]. AI Deployment (0/2): Management talks about biometrics giving 'non-repudiable approvals for material AI agent actions' and is exploring AI-governance partnerships or acquisitions. No AI product or quantified AI savings has shipped [1]. Market Share (0/2): Total revenue is about $8M a year in an IAM market led by Microsoft, Okta, and Ping. Gartner listed BIO-key only as an 'example vendor' in biometric authentication [2]. Pipeline (1/2): Named deployments include a Central Bank of Jordan national biometric initiative, a Portuguese national security agency, and a Saudi education partnership. These are customer wins, not dated next-generation products [1]. R&D Intensity (1/1): Q2 2026 R&D of $640K was about 33% of revenue, above the software-industry average [1].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): BIO-key positions itself as providing secure, phishing-resistant, passwordless identity. That is clear about what it does but not distinct from other IAM vendors [2]. Community Impact (0/2): No charitable or community programs were found [3]. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention data was found. With 41 employees, late 10-K and 10-Q filings that triggered Nasdaq notices in April and June 2026, and repeated equity raises, the company shows no evidence of standout retention [3][5]. Insider Buying (0/2): No net insider buying was found. Recent financing came from a roughly $2.5M warrant inducement that diluted shareholders [1].

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Calculated mechanically as a Growth stock [5]. D/E of 19.9% (1.00), YoY revenue growth of 13.1% (1.00), and Yahoo's Forward P/E of 12.3 (1.00) score at target. The forward P/E rests on thin analyst coverage of a company that has just lost money, so treat it with caution. ROE of -107.9% (0.00, 2x) and profit margin of -90.1% (0.00) reflect continuing losses. The 3-year revenue CAGR derived from reported revenue ($7.02M in 2022 to $5.94M in 2025, -5.4%) scores 0.00 at 2x weight. No PEG is available, so that metric is excluded [5]. Weighted sum is 3.0/8.0, which scales to 3.75 and rounds to 4. The 3-month average volume of 5.44M shares x $2.70 gives about $14.7M of daily dollar volume, which passes the liquidity floor. That volume is spike-driven relative to only 2.04M shares outstanding [5].

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (5/9): AI cuts both ways for BIO-key. AI-driven phishing and deepfakes are increasing demand for phishing-resistant, passwordless authentication; the CEO cites more than 70% of organizations moving to passwordless and tied the October 2026 PortalGuard leadership hire to AI reshaping the identity threat landscape [2]. However, AI-generated spoofs threaten biometric modalities such as face recognition. In addition, platform IAM vendors (Microsoft Entra, Okta) bundle AI-enhanced passkey features, so a sub-scale vendor faces substitution risk [2]. AI Opportunity (0/1): No AI revenue is reported. AI-agent authorization and AI-governance acquisitions are still only ideas [1].

infinite_game.summary: BIO-key has spent 2026 fighting for its listing. It did a reverse split, filed its 10-K and 10-Q late, went through a Nasdaq hearing, and raised money through warrant inducements, while management promises a 'very positive second half' [1][3]. Sinek would recognize a sincere product focus in phishing-resistant identity, but the organization is playing to survive the next deadline rather than to advance a cause [1].

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): Secure, passwordless identity for governments and financial institutions is a worthwhile aim, and wins such as the Central Bank of Jordan initiative serve it [1]. The message is the same as every IAM vendor's, though, and it has not visibly shaped strategy beyond product positioning [2].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): Late annual and quarterly filings that triggered Nasdaq delinquency notices and a delisting hearing in June 2026 point to strained internal capacity at a 41-person company [3][5]. Bringing in an outside cybersecurity executive to run PortalGuard in October 2026 is a sign of turnover rather than a stable, empowered team [2].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Management messaging contrasts BIO-key's methods with others that are 'too vulnerable, too expensive, or too complex to manage at scale'. That frames competitors by their weaknesses rather than as benchmarks [2].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): BIO-key has moved from a fingerprint-hardware company to a software and IAM licensing model, with license fees up 53% and gross margin at 87% in Q2 2026 [1]. The company's 2024 materials called this a 'business transition' that cut revenue 11% that year [2]. The change is real but incremental and was driven partly by financial necessity.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (0/2): Recent decisions were reactive: a reverse split to keep the listing, dilutive warrant inducements, and guidance missed by about 30% in Q2 ($1.92M vs. ~$2.8M) [1][3]. There is no example of a costly long-term bet made from strength.

investment_thesis: The bull case is operating leverage in a niche with tailwinds. 1H 2026 revenue rose 23% to $4.07M, the mix shift to licenses lifted gross margin to 87%, and the 1H net loss improved 59% to $(782K) [1]. National-scale wins (Central Bank of Jordan, a Portuguese national security agency, a Saudi education partnership) and an ~$0.8M hardware order slipped into 2H 2026 support management's target of growth and profitability in the second half [1]. AI-driven phishing and deepfakes are raising demand for phishing-resistant, passwordless authentication, and the ~$2.5M warrant inducement lifted cash above $4.5M [1][2].
thesis_continued: The bear case is scale, governance, and dilution. Revenue of about $8M a year has declined at a -5.4% derived 3-year CAGR, ROE is -107.9%, and profit margin is -90.1% [5]. In 2026 the company missed its 10-K and Q1 10-Q deadlines, received multiple Nasdaq delinquency and bid-price notices, faced a delisting hearing, and needed a 1-for-10 reverse split to stay listed [1][3]. Q2 revenue came in about 30% below the ~$2.8M guidance, and repeated warrant-based financing dilutes holders of a company with about a $5.5M market cap [1][5]. Much larger platform IAM vendors (Microsoft, Okta, Ping) bundle passkeys and biometrics, which limits pricing power [2].
key_catalysts: Q3 2026 results (expected November): delivery on the 2H 2026 revenue-growth and profitability target, including the ~$0.8M hardware order delayed from Q2 [1]
Revenue from the Central Bank of Jordan national biometric authentication initiative and the Portuguese national security agency deployment [1]
A PortalGuard sales push under new president Stephen Morrow (appointed October 2026) to capture enterprise passwordless migration [2]
key_risks: Repeat Nasdaq compliance failures (late filings, bid price) after the 2026 hearing, risking an OTC move [3]
Continued dilution from warrant inducements and equity raises to fund losses at a company with ~$4.5M of cash and ~$5.5M market cap [1][5]
Lumpy government and hardware orders (a single ~$0.8M order equals ~40% of quarterly revenue) causing repeated guidance misses [1]
